key_terms.meaning: The peak arterial pressure, in mmHg, reached just after the ventricles contract
The lowest arterial pressure, in mmHg, just before the next contraction
The tapping sounds heard through a stethoscope over the brachial artery as cuff pressure falls below systolic
MAP ≈ diastolic pressure + (systolic − diastolic)/3, in mmHg
Cardiac output CO = amount of dye injected ÷ (mean concentration × time), the Stewart–Hamilton relation
Cardiac output from the temperature drop seen downstream after injecting a known volume of cold saline
First heart sound, from closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves at the start of systole
Second heart sound, from closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves at the end of systole
A recording of heart sounds and murmurs, usually shown with a simultaneous ECG for timing
A two-channel recording of foetal heart rate and uterine contraction, used in labour
Forced vital capacity: the total volume of air, in litres, blown out as hard and fast as possible after a full breath in
The volume, in litres, exhaled in the first second of a forced expiration
Fraction of the forced vital capacity expelled in one second; normally about 0.75 to 0.80 in adults
Body temperature (37 °C), ambient pressure, saturated with water vapour; lung volumes are reported under these conditions
A flow sensor that reads the small pressure drop across a fixed resistance and converts it to flow
The pressure in the thin space between lung and chest wall, normally slightly below atmospheric
Arterial oxygen saturation estimated from the ratio of red to infrared light absorbed by pulsing blood, given in percent
Breathing measured from the change in electrical impedance across the chest as air enters and leaves the lungs
The volume of air, in litres, left in the lungs after the deepest possible expiration
Raw = (mouth pressure − alveolar pressure) ÷ flow, in cm H₂O per litre per second

takeaways: Blood pressure is always a difference between arterial pressure and the atmosphere, so zeroing the sensor to air is part of every measurement.
The cuff method reads pressure indirectly from Korotkoff sounds; the catheter method reads it directly but needs a sterile artery puncture.
Cardiac output is found from dilution by dividing a known amount of indicator by the area under its downstream concentration-time curve.
Heart sounds are low-frequency events timed to valve closure, and the phonocardiograph is only useful when the sound channel is displayed beside an ECG.
A foetal monitor must reject the mother's much larger ECG or heartbeat before it can count the baby's rate.
Spirometry reports volume and flow under BTPS, and the FEV1/FVC ratio separates an obstructed airway from a stiff lung.
Air flow is measured as a pressure drop; lung and chest pressures are measured to judge how hard the breathing muscles are working.
A pulse oximeter and an impedance apnea monitor are cheap, non-invasive guards for a patient on a hospital bed, and both can be fooled by movement.
A body plethysmograph uses Boyle's law inside a sealed box to find residual volume and airway resistance without asking the patient to cooperate fully.
bank_note: Long answers are asked on the working principle, the block diagram and the sources of error of each instrument, usually with one numerical question on dilution cardiac output or on BTPS correction.

bank.q: Define systolic, diastolic and mean arterial pressure. Describe the auscultatory method of indirect blood pressure measurement and explain what produces each phase of the Korotkoff sounds.
outline: Pressure is measured relative to atmosphere, in mmHg
Cuff placed on upper arm, inflated above systolic to stop flow
Cuff deflated slowly at 2-3 mmHg per second
Turbulent flow under the cuff produces phase 1 tapping sound = systolic
Sound muffling (phase 4) and disappearance (phase 5) = diastolic
Cuff must be at heart level to avoid hydrostatic error
MAP = diastolic + (systolic - diastolic)/3
Sources of error: cuff size, observer hearing, deflation rate

bank.q: Explain the origin of the four heart sounds and describe a phonocardiograph recording system, including the choice between the bell and diaphragm of a stethoscope.
outline: S1 from mitral and tricuspid closure at start of systole
S2 from aortic and pulmonary closure at end of systole
S3 early diastolic filling sound, S4 late diastolic atrial sound
Microphone, low-noise amplifier, band-pass filter of roughly 20-600 Hz
Simultaneous ECG for timing
Bell picks up low frequencies, diaphragm filters them out for higher murmurs
Systole is the interval between S1 and S2, diastole between S2 and the next S1

bank.q: Describe the dye dilution and thermal dilution methods of cardiac output measurement. Give the working equation and list the assumptions.
outline: Indicator injected upstream, concentration sensed downstream
Stewart-Hamilton: CO = amount injected / (mean concentration x time base)
Dye such as indocyanine green, measured by densitometry at the ear or artery
Thermal dilution uses cold saline and a thermistor on a pulmonary artery catheter
Curve must have a clean exponential decay, no recirculation during measurement
Indicator must mix completely and be lost only by flow
Thermal method needs correction for heat loss to catheter wall
Sources of error: injection loss, recirculation, unstable flow

bank.q: Draw and explain a normal forced expiratory spirogram. Define FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC and FEF25-75, and state how the shape separates obstruction from restriction.
outline: Volume-time curve: steep first second, then plateau
FVC = total volume exhaled after full inspiration
FEV1 = volume in first second
Normal FEV1/FVC about 0.75-0.80 in adults
Obstruction: low ratio because FEV1 falls more than FVC
Restriction: normal or high ratio but both FEV1 and FVC reduced
FEF25-75 is the average flow over the middle half of the breath, sensitive to small-airway disease
Flow-volume loop shapes: scooped in obstruction, narrowed in restriction

bank.q: An indicator dilution curve is recorded after injecting 5 mg of dye. The mean concentration over the curve is 2.5 mg per litre and the curve base lasts 12 s. Calculate cardiac output in litres per minute and comment on whether the value is physiological.
outline: CO = amount / (mean concentration x time)
Convert time to minutes: 12 s = 0.2 min
Resting adult value is about 5 L/min, so 10 L/min is high
High output suggests exercise, sepsis, anaemia or a left-to-right shunt
Check injection loss, curve extrapolation and calibration

bank.q: A spirometer calibrated at ATPS reads 3.00 L for a forced vital capacity at 25 °C and 750 mmHg. Describe how the reading is converted to BTPS and explain why the correction is needed. Also list the checks a 3 L calibration syringe is used for.
outline: BTPS = body temperature 37 °C, ambient pressure, water vapour saturated
Gas expands as it warms from 25 °C to 37 °C
BTPS factor from standard tables, roughly 1.08 at this temperature and pressure
Corrected FVC approximately 3.24 L
Reason: the lung reports volumes at body conditions, so clinic readings must match
Syringe used to check linearity, leaks, and volume accuracy of the sensor
Also check that a known 3 L push reads about 3 L on the display

bank.q: A screen pneumotachometer has a resistance of 2 cm H₂O per litre per second and shows a pressure drop of 6 cm H₂O. Find the flow. Explain how the signal is made linear and how volume is obtained from it.
outline: Flow = pressure drop / resistance = 6/2 = 3 L/s
Flow is proportional to pressure drop only when the flow profile is laminar (Poiseuille)
Capillary or screen element keeps flow laminar
Two symmetric pressure taps allow bidirectional measurement
Flow is electronically integrated to give volume
Drift of the integrator needs a reset or a high-pass zero
Gas condition affects viscosity, so BTPS correction applies

bank.q: A two-wavelength pulse oximeter measures the ratio of ratios R = 0.6. Explain how R is formed, how it is converted to SpO2, and describe three situations in which the reading becomes unreliable.
outline: Red and infrared LEDs alternately illuminate the finger
Photodiode current has a steady and a pulsatile part
Ratio uses the pulsatile (AC) divided by steady (DC) part at each wavelength
R = AC/DC at red divided by AC/DC at infrared
R is mapped to SpO2 through a calibration curve from volunteer studies
Unreliable with poor perfusion, motion artefact, nail polish or bright light
Carboxyhaemoglobin and methaemoglobin read falsely high or low

bank.q: Compare direct and indirect methods of blood pressure measurement. Discuss which is chosen in an intensive care unit, in a home UPI-era health check, and during exercise testing, giving reasons.
outline: Direct: catheter in artery with strain-gauge or fluid-coupled transducer, continuous waveform, gold standard
Direct risks: infection, thrombosis, bleeding, needs trained staff
Indirect: cuff with auscultation, oscillometry or ultrasound, non-invasive, intermittent
Indirect errors: cuff size, arrhythmia, calcified arteries, observer bias
ICU uses direct arterial line for beat-to-beat values and drug titration
Home and clinic use automated oscillometric cuff devices
Exercise testing needs fast repeated readings, so automated cuffs or finger methods are used
Conclusion: choice depends on need for continuity, accuracy and risk

bank.q: Describe a foetal monitoring system based on abdominal ECG and phonocardiography. Explain how the foetal signal is separated from the maternal signal and how the arrhythmia monitor in the same unit measures RR intervals.
outline: Abdominal electrodes pick up both maternal and foetal ECG
Foetal R wave is smaller; maternal complexes are removed by subtraction or gating
Foetal heart rate computed from foetal RR interval, about 110-160 beats per minute
Ultrasound Doppler and foetal phonocardiography are alternatives
Cardiotocograph plots foetal rate against uterine contractions
Arrhythmia monitor measures each RR interval and compares with running average
Alarm when rate crosses limits or RR changes abruptly
Artefacts: movement, electrode loss, missed R waves; need blanking and averaging

bank.q: A body plethysmograph is used to measure thoracic gas volume and airway resistance. Explain the principle with Boyle's law, derive the volume equation, and discuss why the panting manoeuvre is used.
outline: Patient sits in a sealed box and breathes through a shutter and mouthpiece
Shutter closes and the patient pants against it
Alveolar gas is compressed and rarefied, mouth pressure tracks alveolar pressure
Box pressure changes oppositely as box volume changes
Boyle's law: P1V1 = P2V2 applied to the gas in the chest and to the box
Thoracic gas volume obtained, residual volume = thoracic gas volume minus expiratory reserve volume
Shutter open, flow and mouth pressure give airway resistance from pressure-flow slope
Panting keeps gas exchange and temperature effects small

bank.q: Design a bedside monitoring chain for a post-operative patient that continuously shows ECG, SpO2, blood pressure and breathing. State what each channel measures, how alarms are set, and how artefacts are reduced.
outline: ECG electrodes with high common-mode rejection amplifier and driven right leg
SpO2 finger probe with ratio-of-ratios processing
Blood pressure by automated cuff, or arterial line if continuous values are needed
Respiration from chest impedance bands between ECG electrodes
Alarm limits set from the patient's baseline with delay to avoid false calls
Artefacts: movement, mains interference, electrode drying, poor perfusion
Use of filters, averaging, lead-off detection and signal quality indicators
Isolation barrier for patient safety and defibrillation protection

bank.q: Compare the pneumotachometer, the spirometer and the impedance method for measuring ventilation. Discuss accuracy, patient effort and suitability for long-term apnea monitoring.
outline: Pneumotachometer gives true flow from a pressure drop, needs a mouthpiece and is accurate but interferes with breathing
Spirometer integrates flow or volume directly, used for forced manoeuvres in the clinic
Impedance method is non-contact apart from surface electrodes, gives relative change not absolute volume
Impedance is best for apnea alarm, not for lung function numbers
Movement and cardiac pulsation corrupt the impedance signal
Choice depends on whether absolute volume or a trend is needed
A 3 L syringe check is standard for spirometer and pneumotachograph chains

glossary.def: Listening to body sounds, here the Korotkoff sounds over an artery below a cuff.
Automated cuff method that reads pressure from the size of the pressure pulsations in the cuff.
A diaphragm whose resistance changes when pressure bends it, used in direct blood pressure lines.
Volume of blood pumped by the heart per minute, about 5 L/min at rest in an adult.
Blood flow equals the amount of a substance taken up per minute divided by the arteriovenous concentration difference.
A dye used for dilution cardiac output, measured optically because it absorbs near 800 nm.
The part of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles contract and eject blood.
The part of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles relax and fill.
The cup-shaped chest piece of a stethoscope, best for low-frequency sounds such as S3 and S4.
The flat chest piece of a stethoscope, which filters low frequencies and highlights murmurs.
Any abnormal rhythm, detected by comparing each RR interval with set limits.
Time between two successive R waves of the ECG, in milliseconds; inverse gives heart rate.
The baby's heart rate, normally about 110 to 160 beats per minute.
Instrument that records the volume of air breathed in and out and the speed of the breath.
A spirometer design in which a piston rolls on a flexible seal with low friction, giving an accurate volume signal.
Ambient temperature and pressure, saturated with water vapour; conditions at the spirometer itself.
The highest flow, in litres per minute, reached during a forced expiration.
Volume that can still be breathed out after a normal quiet expiration.
Method that finds lung volume from the dilution of a known amount of helium in a closed circuit.
Pressure inside the air sacs, equal to atmospheric when no air is moving.
A pause in breathing, commonly alarming when it lasts longer than about 10 to 20 seconds.
Optical recording of the pulsatile blood volume in a finger or earlobe.
At constant temperature, pressure times volume of a fixed amount of gas stays constant.
A sealed box in which pressure changes around a breathing subject give lung volume and airway resistance.
